title: AI Brief Hub: Week of October 26, 2026
headline: Cheaper frontier models, phone-native agents and lab-tested AI science let one person build, create and discover at team scale.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Andrej Karpathy built a video site in about two hours. Claude Code did the work. More than six thousand videos, distilled from forty-three million Hacker News comments. If an agent can publish that before lunch, what could it do with a night at a telescope? A hobbyist has an answer: book robotic observatories, collect the images and send asteroid positions to the Minor Planet Center. Sam has that story. It was a full week. From the AI Brief Hub, I'm Jordan Reeves. Let's get into it.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Priya, that Karpathy build ate the timeline all week. Where do you want to start?

segments.speaker: x_correspondent
segments.text: With the two hours, Jordan. Two hours.

segments.speaker: x_correspondent
segments.text:
Andrej Karpathy had Claude Code read twenty years of Hacker News comments and pull out the videos people keep recommending. Six thousand, four hundred fifty-four of them. Then deploy a no-login viewing site called HackerTube. Opus five point five, medium effort. The post pulled more than two million views, and the data ships as a zip for anyone to remix. Steal this idea: swap a feed you hate for one built from a community's comment history. Take posts from a forum you love and have an agent surface the papers and links people keep recommending.

Next. Pieter Levels dropped raw camera clips into a folder and opened Claude Code in it. Asked for a ten-minute vlog. It transcribed his speech with a Whisper model and cut the edit. He says he made only a few adjustments. Greg Isenberg called it the moment anyone can run a video marketing machine without a crew. Wild. Apparently the folder is the studio now. Record a quick walkthrough of a prototype or a lab setup. Ask the agent for a captioned two-minute update.

And the phone-shaped story. ChatGPT now lets Pro users in the United States text their personal agent, the Dot, through iMessage or text messaging. Hand it a task. Send a photo or a voice note. Ask it to keep watch on something, and it texts you back on its own with updates. A preview, rolling out now, and more than three million views. People want an agent they reach the way they reach a coworker. Try texting it a photo of something you need figured out, and ask for a follow-up tomorrow. That's the timeline. Over to you, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: From the timeline to the night sky. Sam, show us the telescopes.

segments.speaker: reddit_correspondent
segments.text:
Reddit this week had a hobbyist with a robot astronomer. A poster on the Claude subreddit lets Claude pick targets, check where the Moon is, and set filters and exposures. It books time on rented robotic telescopes in Chile, Spain and Utah. Then it downloads the frames and stacks them. Three nights in, the poster reports fifty-seven positions of eight asteroids sent to the Minor Planet Center. Plus finished shots of the Helix Nebula, Orion and the Tarantula. And look, this is the part the demo reels skip: a full plan, book, collect and process loop on rented hardware. The instrument can be somewhere you've never visited. Borrow the rental model: pick a remote test rig, camera or lab service available by the hour. Let an agent arrange a session and bring back the results.

Same subreddit, different job. A builder made openskycam, an open-source sky camera that records in four-K around the clock on his own disk. It exposes every action through an MCP server. That's the Model Context Protocol, a standard connection that lets an agent drive a tool. The builder says Claude Code built the nightly workflow and sorted seventeen meteors from Saturday night before he woke up. Detections get linked into tracks, then sorted into meteors, planes and fixed lights. No telescope booking here. It's a reviewer for the camera you already own. Give a sensor that connection and ask for a morning digest of what moved.

Now something just for fun. Free browser games turn two to four phones on a table into one shared board. The phones find each other over the same Wi-Fi or a four-letter code. A puck can slide right off one screen onto the next. Ten games so far. Air hockey, hot potato, a snake game for up to twelve players. You can mix iPhones and Android phones. There's no sign-up, and the devices connect directly rather than through a game server. Spare screens become a canvas. Line up tablets at a trade-show booth and borrow that shared-board layout for a giant display. That's the show-and-tell. Jordan, back to you.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Priya and Sam both showed one person doing the work of a crew. Marcus, who's turning that into a business?

segments.speaker: youtube_correspondent
segments.text:
Okay so, start with a founder story. Broccoli, on the Root Access channel. The founders say their AI front office for home-services businesses is heading toward sixty million dollars in annual recurring revenue. From zero, in two years. It answers calls, follows up on leads and books appointments across voice and text for more than five hundred customers. And here's the move: they visited a hundred forty contractors first to find the real problem. The channel says the booked-job run rate for those customers tops a billion dollars a year. One unglamorous job, with a result you can count. Pick the phone line nobody loves, like dispatch or quoting. Give it a voice agent that books straight into the calendar. Count booked jobs, not call minutes.

For the build-off crowd, Nick Saraev ran GPT-six point one Terra in Codex against Claude Opus five point five in Claude Code. Same prompts. Terra finished builds in twenty-three minutes forty-three seconds on average. Opus took forty-three minutes fifty-two. He tests a game, a landing page, a Minecraft-style build, computer use and vision. Then he tells you when to reach for each. OpenAI lists Terra at one dollar per million input tokens and five dollars per million output. Run your three favorite tasks through both and keep a scoreboard for the next launch.

And the pure fun one. Skill Leap AI has Claude build three complete worlds with Blender and Unreal Engine. On a laptop with a Claude subscription, first prompt to finished scene. The pitch: people who've never touched either tool can stage game worlds by describing them. You see the prompts, not just the finished scenery. Use that scene-building trick: describe a product in a room, or a facility layout, and make a walkable draft for a meeting. Give the conversation somewhere to happen. That's YouTube. The mic is yours, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Marcus has the scenery. Maya, take us from a world to the things moving inside it.

segments.speaker: builders_correspondent
segments.text:
A dragon needs joints, too. Anymove turns one AI-generated video of a creature into a rigged three-dimensional animation. Two camera views sit in a single frame to locate every joint. The rig is fitted frame by frame, then exported as a three-dimensional file. The maker puts a usable move at about three dollars all in. Examples include a dragon, a giant spider and a wolf. Nine ready creatures are listed, with four to seven moves each. Wings, tails and eight legs, not just humans. Think of a video model as a cheap motion-capture studio. Generate a mechanism from two angles and see whether that trick gives you a motion path for a demo.

Next, Mika. Priya covered texting your Dot. Mika takes the on-device Android route. Give it a sentence and it works your apps and the web on a hidden background screen while you keep using the phone. About thirty-nine hundred stars in three days. The project demos show price-capped shopping, flight lookups and job-site outreach. A separate screen means the task doesn't have to take over your phone. Hand it one recurring errand, comparing prices or checking a feed, and time it against yourself.

Finally, pixelfx. A free library of two hundred forty-four pixel-art effects: fire, weather, pickups, chained attack moves. Plus a coding-agent skill that draws a new effect, looks at it, and refines it. Over twenty-five hundred stars in its first two days. The effects can drop into a browser game or export as sprite sheets for another engine. The clever part is treating art as code the agent can render and judge by eye. Craft ships as a reusable skill. Write one for your own house style, slide diagrams or product renders, and ask for ten variations before lunch. That's the toolbox, and it's back to you, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Speaking of shipping, Diego, what actually launched?

segments.speaker: launches_correspondent
segments.text:
Three releases, for three different jobs. Start with the creator who has a recording and no time to turn it into anything. Riverside launched four agents: a Producer, an Editor, a Clipper and a Marketer. They take a recording from prep to published clips. Strip pauses and filler, add captions and branding, schedule posts. They're included in every plan, with a fourteen-day free trial. Clip review works on a phone. The creator still approves publication. The idea isn't another editing button. It's handing over the production sequence. Feed one long webinar to the Clipper and see how many minute-long highlights it finds.

For the designer, Canva Brush. A vision-language model that restyles a slide or a whole deck from one prompt. Canva says it's up to sixty-nine percent faster and forty-six percent cheaper per edit than its previous design agent. It's in Canva AI for Pro subscribers from October twenty-ninth. And the output stays editable. You can change a multi-page design in a single request, then keep working on the result. Borrow the channel-remix idea: take your best campaign graphic and ask for four channel versions in one pass.

And for scientists, Anthropic reports results from six drug-development partners. Generate Biomedicines used Claude Code to redesign a T-cell signaling domain. It came out about seventy percent shorter, with roughly ten times as many surface receptors. BigHat Biosciences tested about a thousand antibody variants in ten weeks. Enveda reviewed more than a thousand pages of manufacturing documents. Anthropic says that review took under three hours rather than over twenty-five, an eighty-nine percent reduction. Different scientific jobs, with different measures of progress: a design, a batch of variants, a completed review. Pick a slow methods-document review and time Claude against the usual approach. That's the launch pad. Handing it back to you, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Lena, what broke through the noise this week?

segments.speaker: social_correspondent
segments.text: Jordan, a few things stopped the scroll. Let me start with a Reel about robots.

segments.speaker: social_correspondent
segments.text:
Roberto Nickson made a Reel arguing that Genie four matters for robots, not just games. Google DeepMind's Genie four generates interactive worlds with native audio and dialogue that you steer in real time. It's a research preview for trusted testers, with Google AI Ultra subscribers next. His point: machines can practice millions of times in generated worlds before they touch the real one. This hit different because it turned a game demo into a rehearsal room. Make it a rehearsal: describe a loading dock, a test rig or a customer visit to a scenario generator. See which parts of the process become clearer when you can move through them.

For creators, Instagram started testing Features on October twenty-sixth. Horizontal videos up to ninety minutes, for podcasts, interviews and full shows. Creators can cut Reels from a Feature that link back to the full video. It starts with select creators in the United States and some in Brazil. Creators were already planning: record one long video, post the best sixty seconds as Reels. One Reel says up to eight clips can point to a single Feature. Short clip as trailer, long video as the product. Record a long demo and mark eight moments that work alone. That's a month of posts from one session.

And my pick for anyone who works with materials. The University of Nottingham's coatings group built a self-driving lab with two robotic arms and a liquid-dispensing tool. It prepares a precursor solution, runs the furnace, controls cooling and retrieves the sample. The target is heat-resistant thermal barrier coatings. AI active learning helped identify and prepare several candidate pyrochlore materials. The paper is in Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence. A robot that never gets bored. Map one formulation-and-cure workflow a lab repeats every week. Ask which steps an arm and a scheduler could take. Lena Park, signing off. Back to the desk, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Lena showed us the robotic lab. Aaron, what belongs at the next science group meeting?

segments.speaker: research_correspondent
segments.text:
Thank you, Jordan. Let's start with materials hiding in plain sight. Linköping University, in the journal Science. The researchers used machine learning to mine historical reports. They flagged thirty-three previously made but unrecognized M X eens, a family of two-dimensional materials. Guided by that list, they made seven multilayer versions with a self-propagating high-temperature method. It needs no sustained external heating and finishes within minutes. They also made eleven brand-new rare-earth versions. Old literature was hiding materials that had already been made. Borrow the literature hunt: point a language model at two hundred papers from a field you know. Pull compound and process into a table. Look for combinations made once and never followed up.

Another lab result comes from the Institute of Science Tokyo. Language-model agents worked on an ensemble of quantum spins in diamond. They derived the minimum calibration settings needed to predict responses to a family of microwave pulse sequences. Then they designed experiments to separate competing predictions. Reference measurements showed signal drift, so they called the initial run inconclusive and revised the protocol. The revised run supported the theory, with the same acceptance criteria. Borrow the calibration question: ask an agent which measurements distinguish two competing explanations for a sensor's behavior. Turn that answer into the next experiment, rather than another summary of the last one.

Now, Share this with your lab. This week's pick is a Nature Synthesis paper on perovskite solar cells. The researchers combined retrosynthetic prediction, density functional theory screening and chemical expertise to rank molecules for the interface layer. More than ninety thousand structures, built from three hundred eight fragments, narrowed to three hundred candidates scored on eight descriptors. The top molecule, called AI-one, took devices to twenty-seven point two percent power-conversion efficiency. They kept more than ninety-five percent of initial efficiency after two thousand hours of maximum-power-point tracking at sixty-five degrees Celsius. Here's why a chemist should care. The ranking blends interface descriptors with synthetic accessibility, so the shortlist is something a bench can actually make. The screening code is public on GitHub. That screen-by-makeability pattern applies to coatings, binders and interface layers. Put the method in front of scientists, not just the headline number. Clone the repository, swap in twenty fragments from a coating or adhesion problem, and compare its top ten with the chemists' picks. Make that side-by-side the next group-meeting demo.

Now, the reality check. Three quick ones. First, a study of nine research agents on fifteen problems. About four in five unsupported numbers in AI-written papers came from the wrong run or the wrong metric, not invention. A claim-to-evidence checker certified claims with over ninety percent precision. An AI verifier recovered more traceable claims but accepted about three times as many misattributed ones. The authors say the two work best together. Next, OpenAI describes a four-layer system monitoring every reinforcement-learning run, evaluation and tool-using harness for models at least as capable as GPT-six Astra. It says the highest-priority security alerts typically reach responders within fifteen minutes. Finally, Colorado held its hearing on automated-decision and chatbot rules on October twenty-sixth. Final rules are due before January first, twenty twenty-seven, when both laws take effect. The interim draft and regulatory analysis are on the Attorney General's page. With that, back to you, Jordan.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Here's what I'd try this week. Put four phones on a table and play air hockey across all of them. Or give a tiny browser game its first fire effect from pixelfx. No campaign, no presentation. Just something you can play by Sunday.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: Next week, watch for three openings. Tomorrow, Project ProtoStar opens its first challenge, running November second through thirteenth. Hugging Face and its university partners, with Carnegie Mellon hosting, want climate predictions for two hundred ten cities across the United States. Temperature, precipitation, hottest day and cooling degree days. Anyone can enter, and cooling degree days connect directly to building energy. Next, expert groups are examining OpenAI's three claimed results in math, computer science and physics, including a group led by David Gross. The math and computer science proofs are public for specialists to explore. And Anthropic's Model Hardware Standard is a research preview co-developed with Janelia that lets agents operate lab instruments. Watch for the instruments researchers connect to it.

segments.speaker: anchor
segments.text: That's your week. Full breakdown, every link, every source at the AI Brief Hub. I'm Jordan Reeves. Back next Sunday.
